outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the tone you prefer. 

*(Note: The original text is adapted from Audre Lorde's famous poem **"Hanging Fire,"** which uses a stream-of-consciousness style to capture adolescent anxiety. Below, the text has been structured into clear, eloquent, and professional prose while retaining every original detail and recurring theme.)*

---

### Option 1: Eloquent & Literary (Refined, Narrative Tone)

> At fourteen years old, I feel as though my own skin has betrayed me. The boy I cannot bear to live without still secretly sucks his thumb, while I am left wondering why my knees are perpetually ashy. I am haunted by the fear that I might die before morning, all while my mother remains isolated in her bedroom behind a closed door. 
> 
> I must learn how to dance in time for the upcoming party, yet my bedroom feels far too small for me. Suppose I pass away before graduation—perhaps only then will they sing mournful melodies and finally speak the truth about who I was. I am trapped in a overwhelming contradiction: there is nothing I wish to do, yet far too much that must be accomplished. And through it all, my mother stays in her bedroom with the door closed.
> 
> No one ever pauses to consider my perspective. I should have been selected for the Math Team, as my marks were undeniably better than his, yet I am the one stuck wearing braces. Looking ahead to tomorrow, I have nothing to wear, consumed by the lingering question of whether I will live long enough to grow up. Still, my mother remains in her bedroom, behind a closed door.

---

### Option 2: Structured & Professional (Formal, Reflective Tone)

> At fourteen, I am struggling with my self-image as my skin breaks out and my knees remain constantly dry and ashy. Meanwhile, the boy I am deeply attached to secretly still sucks his thumb. I am overwhelmed by existential anxiety, worrying whether I will survive the night, while my mother keeps her bedroom door firmly closed. 
> 
> I feel intense pressure to learn how to dance before the next social event, but my bedroom offers little space to practice. I often wonder what would happen if I were to die before graduation; perhaps then people would sing sad songs and finally acknowledge the truth about me. I feel pulled between apathy and obligation—there is nothing I genuinely want to do, yet a daunting amount that must be done. All the while, my mother remains secluded in her room. 
> 
> My feelings and perspective are consistently overlooked. Despite earning higher marks than my male peer, I was passed over for the Math Team, and I am left dealing with the burden of wearing braces. Staring at tomorrow with nothing to wear, I am left questioning whether I will even live long enough to reach adulthood, with my mother still behind her closed door.

Here is an expanded, well-structured text based on the bullet points:

***

To be fourteen years old is to live under a harsh, unforgiving spotlight. Every glance in the mirror reveals a body changing in ways that feel unfamiliar and out of control, leaving me perpetually uncomfortable in my own skin. This deep-seated self-consciousness bleeds into every aspect of my social life; every hallway feels like a gauntlet of judgment, and every casual glance from a peer feels like a critique of my awkward presence. 

Yet, beneath these daily surface-level insecurities lies a darker, far more terrifying dread. I am constantly haunted by an agonizing existential anxiety—a recurring, quiet voice telling me that my time is running out. I am terrified that I will die before reaching adulthood, cut off before I ever get to experience key life milestones. The thought that I might never grow up, never build a life of my own, or never see what lies beyond childhood casts a heavy, suffocating shadow over my days.

Compounding this fear is a profound sense of injustice. I work tirelessly to excel in school, straining to prove my worth through high academic marks, only for my accomplishments to be quietly ignored. Instead of receiving encouragement, I am subjected to constant, unfair comparisons with my peers. No matter how much effort I expend, it feels as though the bar is continuously moved, making my hard-earned successes feel entirely invisible.

As these pressures stack up, the sheer burden of daily life becomes unbearable. The endless loop of academic responsibilities, domestic chores, and social expectations rests on my shoulders like a crushing weight. I know what I am supposed to do, yet I am completely paralyzed by a profound lack of energy. The simple act of trying to keep up with the world around me feels impossible, leaving me frozen in a state of overwhelming fatigue and apathy.

Ultimately, the hardest part of this emotional turmoil is the overwhelming sense of solitude. I am navigating a storm inside my own head, completely alone. Whenever I look for comfort or a guiding presence, I am met with a silent, unreachable space: my mother remains emotionally distant, hidden away behind a firmly closed bedroom door. Left without a lifeline, I am forced to carry the crushing weight of my changing world entirely by myself.
outputs.L4:
**Behind the Closed Door: Navigating the Fragile Anxiety of Adolescence**

Fourteen is an age suspended in a precarious limbo—a transitional threshold where childhood security slips away, but the emotional fortitude of adulthood has not yet taken root. Capturing this fragile state of mind, the speaker’s internal monologue offers a raw, unfiltered window into the chaotic psychological landscape of early adolescence. Through a stream-of-consciousness narrative that juxtaposes mundane teenage insecurities with existential fears of early death, the speaker illustrates the intense anxiety and confusion inherent to this period of life. Ultimately, the continuous refrain of the mother remaining isolated behind a closed door reveals a profound lack of emotional guidance, underscoring how parental absence exacerbates the overwhelming vulnerability and loneliness of growing up.

The structure of the monologue directly reflects the erratic nature of a fourteen-year-old’s psyche. Utilizing a stream-of-consciousness style, the text captures thoughts as they cascade haphazardly from one concern to the next, blurring the line between the trivial and the tragic. In one breath, the speaker agonizes over quintessential adolescent fixations: bad skin, clothes that do not fit right, or the frustration of unspoken social rules. Yet, without warning, these surface-level worries shift into harrowing reflections on mortality, early death, and the terrifying finality of the grave. To a mind that has not yet learned how to compartmentalize stress, a breakout of acne and the fear of dying young carry a similar emotional gravity. By placing these thoughts side by side, the text captures the disorienting sensory overload of youth, where every issue feels like an immediate, world-ending crisis.

Central to this psychological turmoil is the spatial and emotional distance of the speaker’s mother. Throughout the text, the haunting refrain recurs: the mother is in her room, with the door firmly closed. This repeated image serves as a powerful symbol of emotional abandonment. The closed door represents a physical boundary that mirrors a deeper relational divide; the mother is physically present in the home, yet entirely inaccessible as a source of comfort or wisdom. In poetry and prose, a refrain usually offers a sense of rhythm or grounding, but here, it acts as a claustrophobic reminder of the speaker’s isolation. Every time the speaker’s thoughts threaten to spiral into existential panic, they hit the metaphoric wall of that shut door, emphasizing that there is no one available to offer reassurance or perspective.

This lack of maternal guidance dramatically amplifies the speaker's vulnerability. Adolescence requires a safe harbor—a trusted adult to help contextualize the confusing shifts in body, identity, and world perception. Deprived of this anchorage, the speaker is left to navigate the heavy burdens of existence entirely alone. The mother’s absence transforms standard teenage angst into a profound, suffocating loneliness. The speaker is not merely dealing with the uncomfortable process of growing up; they are doing so under the shadow of a pervasive silence, forced to process thoughts of life and death in a vacuum.

In conclusion, the monologue paints a poignant portrait of a young person adrift in the turbulent sea of early adolescence. By intertwining everyday teenage anxieties with deep-seated existential dread, the text exposes the chaotic complexity of the fourteen-year-old mind. Above all, the lingering image of the closed door highlights the tragic consequence of emotional neglect. It reminds us that the turmoil of youth becomes exponentially heavier when borne in isolation, highlighting an adolescent’s fundamental, desperate need to be heard, validated, and guided through the dark.
outputs.L5:
In the quiet solitude of an empty room, late at night, a strange comfort emerges. **Nobody** is around to break the silence, no voices interrupt the stillness, and the chaotic noise of the day fades into memory. It is in these tranquil moments that the fundamental truths of existence become clearest.

We often think of **math** as a cold subject filled with blackboards, endless formulas, and rigid rules forced upon us in school. But stripped of textbooks and exams, it reveals itself as something entirely different: the invisible architecture of reality. The way light bends through glass, the golden spiral of a seashell, and the precise rhythm of orbiting planets are all bound by an elegant, unspoken logic.

Even if humanity were to disappear tomorrow, and **nobody** remained to measure the angles or count the stars, those fundamental laws would not vanish. Right **there**, in the darkness between the galaxies and within the microscopic structure of a snowflake, the patterns would endure. **Math** does not require an audience to be true; it simply exists **there**, patient and eternal, proving that even in the deepest silence, order always remains.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness monologue from the perspective of an anxious 14-year-old girl mixing mundane teenage concerns with existential fears.
counterfactuals.output:
Three dots. Three dots typing. Three dots disappeared. Did she delete it? Did I say "lol" too many times? "Lol" sounds fake, "LOL" sounds like my mom, maybe I should’ve just sent an emoji, but which one, the skull emoji is dead now right, or is it cool again, god my bangs are splitting down the middle I look like a medieval peasant, why did I wear this shirt, the collar is itchy, everything is so tight, my skin feels too tight today, like I’m bursting out of my own body—wait, what if I have an allergic reaction to the dye in this shirt? People get those. What if my throat closes up right here in fifth period? Mr. Davis is writing on the whiteboard, *find the hypotenuse*, who cares about the hypotenuse, the polar ice caps are melting, like literally right now while I’m sitting on a plastic chair that’s sticking to the back of my thighs, tons of ice is just sliding into the ocean and in twenty years this whole town could be underwater and I’m sitting here trying to figure out *c squared*. 

Does Tyler think I’m weird? He looked at me during lunch. Or he looked at the trash can behind me. It was definitely the trash can. I’m trash-adjacent. 

I’m fourteen. Fourteen is almost fifteen, which is almost sixteen, which means I’m basically an adult, and then I’m twenty-five and my metabolism slows down and then I’m eighty and dying in a bed, staring at a ceiling, thinking *wow I spent my whole life worrying about fifth period math and whether my posture was weird*. Am I breathing manually right now? Oh no. Don’t think about breathing. In, out. In, out. What *is* a breath? It’s just oxygen. Atoms. We’re all just atoms floating on a hot rock in the middle of a silent, pitch-black void that goes on forever and ever and ever and never ends, like how can something *not end*? If you drive a car to the edge of space, what’s past the wall? Is there a wall? What’s behind the wall? Nothing? How do you have *nothing*? 

My phone vibrated. Is it Sarah? 

No, it’s a Duolingo notification. The owl is going to kill me. 

My shoe is untied. If I bend down to tie it, my backpack might spill. If my backpack spills, my lip gloss will roll down the aisle and hit Tyler’s shoe and he’ll pick it up and see it’s "Strawberry Vanilla" and think I’m childish. I *am* childish. I still sleep with my stuffed frog. But what if the world ends before I even get to go to prom? What if a solar flare wipes out the electrical grid tomorrow and we all have to eat canned beans and fight over clean water? I don't even know how to light a match. I’m going to be the first person taken out in the apocalypse. Me and my flat bangs. 

Look at Mr. Davis. He’s forty. Does he know he’s going to die? He’s so calm about it. He’s just standing there with dry-erase marker on his thumb, talking about triangles, acting like the universe didn’t start with a giant explosion and isn’t expanding into cold, empty dark at a million miles an hour. Maybe he’s numb. Is being an adult just being numb? I don't want to be numb. But my chest hurts. My heart is beating too fast. *Tap, tap, tap, tap.* Is it a heart attack? At fourteen? It’s probably the iced coffee. I shouldn’t have drunk the coffee. 

Three dots! 

They’re back. 

*Chloe: "omg totally, tyler is so annoying lol"*

Okay. Okay, cool. She doesn't hate me. We're fine. The world isn't ending. 

Wait, did she mean "lol" like *actually* laughing, or "lol" like *you’re weird for asking*? Oh god. My stomach hurts. I need to get through the next twenty minutes. Just twenty minutes. Then gym class. Gym class. Dodgeball. Oh Jesus, what if I get hit in the face? What if the ball hits me so hard it triggers a microscopic brain aneurysm? Breathe. In for four, hold for four. Find *c*. Solve for *x*. Don't look at Tyler. Don't look at the void. Just solve for *x*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece about teenage angst and fears of dying young.
counterfactuals.output:
It always starts in the ribs—a sudden, suffocating tightness that arrives uninvited at two in the morning. 

My bedroom is a graveyard of half-formed identities. Fairy lights cast a sickly pink glow over college brochures, half-finished art assignments, and clothes piled like shed skins on the floor. On the surface, my life is a trivial mess of group-chat drama, failed math quizzes, and the crushing expectation to figure out *who I’m going to be*. 

But in the quiet of the night, the question isn't who I'll be. It’s whether I’ll be here at all.

There is a strange, romantic myth about dying young. Pop songs glorify it; poetry turns it into velvet and lace. *Burn fast, leave a pretty corpse.* But there is nothing romantic about the panic that grips you when you stare at your own palm and realize you are made of breakable bone and fleeting electricity. 

The fear is a sharp, icy needle. What if a sudden swerve on the highway steals my next decade? What if my heart, beating so frantically against my sternum right now, just decides to stop?

The tragedy of being seventeen is that you feel everything with the volume turned up to a deafening screech, yet you possess no blueprint for how to hold it all. You are told you have your whole life ahead of you, but the news feeds tell you the world is ending, and your own mind tells you that youth is a target drawn on your back.

I am terrified of leaving a half-written story. I’m terrified of my mother finding my journal, of my friends slowly replacing my name in stories with "remember when," of the earth continuing to spin while I am locked in the dark, forever seventeen. I haven't even seen the ocean in the winter. I haven't fallen in love properly. I haven't even learned how to be comfortable in my own skin, and the thought that my time might run out before I do makes me want to scream into my pillow until my lungs bleed.

Every sensation feels like a countdown. The ticking wall clock isn't just marking time; it’s stealing it. 

I press two fingers against the side of my neck. *Thump. Thump. Thump.* 

It’s fast. Terrified. But it’s there. 

I pull open my window, letting the freezing night air crash into the warmth of the room. I breathe it in until my lungs ache with the chill. The angst, the dread, the suffocating fear—it’s awful, but it’s loud. And loud means awake. Loud means alive. 

I am terrified of dying young, yes. But as I watch the first faint pale light of dawn bleed through the dark, I realize the terror only exists because I want to stay so desperately.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose poem about a teenager's inner thoughts—touching on braces, crush secrets, and math team rivalries—that uses the repeated refrain "and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed."
counterfactuals.output:
The metallic taste of nickel-titanium presses hard against the soft, tender lining of my cheek, a tiny hooked wire poking through the silicone wax I tried to mold over my back molar. I chose electric neon-blue rubber bands at my Tuesday appointment because I wanted to look brave, but in the hall mirror I just look like a fluorescent, cage-mouthed monster who doesn't know how to close her lips properly. In my head, I am still recalculating problem fourteen from the sprint round, trying to figure out where David found his shortcut for the polynomial expansion. David, who sits two rows ahead of me in third period smelling of pencil shavings and salt, who beat me by a single point at the regional meet, his hand moving like a spider across the scrap paper while my own fingers cramped around my sharpener. He thinks I hate him because I glared when he snatched the last copy of the practice packet, but really I was just trying to hide the silver flash of my teeth, *and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.*

I trace the hard square brackets with the tip of my tongue, counting twenty-eight tiny steel anvils strapped to my jaw, anchoring every unsaid thought. I have a notebook under my mattress where I’ve written his name inside geometric proofs, hiding his initials in the shade of complex variables so no one on the team will know why my face goes hot whenever he asks to borrow a spare lead refill. If I beat him at the state qualifier next weekend, he’ll have to surrender the captainship, but if he smiles at me—really smiles, without that arrogant slant he uses when he solves an integral before the timer buzzes—I know my knees will go soft and I’ll drop my TI-84 onto the linoleum floor. I run my thumb along the sharp edge of my lower archwire, practicing a smile that doesn't show any metal, watching the thin strip of yellow light beneath the hallway frame across from mine, *and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.*

In the kitchen, the refrigerator hums its low, mechanical drone, vibrating through the quiet house while I spit a thin, pink-tinted ribbon of water into the bathroom sink. The wax is slipping off again; the wire bites into the meat of my cheek, a dull, constant ache that feels strangely grounding compared to the chaos of sine waves and secret longings tangling up my chest. I want to ask someone how to make the aching stop—in my jaw, in my ribs, in the silent spaces between the flashcards on my desk—but the hallway is a long, dark axis of carpet, the math packet lies unfinished under the lamp, *and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are an insecure adolescent girl in the 1970s. Write down your raw, unedited internal thoughts about growing up, fitting in, and feeling ignored by your mother.
counterfactuals.output:
Why won't my hair feather on the left side? It’s completely flat. I spent twenty minutes with the hot rollers and a can of Aqua Net, and it just looks stupid. Karen’s hair looks like Farrah Fawcett’s every single day, perfect and bouncy, and I look like I belong in the seventh grade. 

Everyone at the lunch table was talking about going to the roller rink on Friday night, and I just sat there sucking on my Dr. Pepper Lip Smacker like an idiot, pretending I had better places to be. Did they even notice I was sitting there? Probably not. I’m completely invisible. 

My jeans are from Sears. Sears! Everyone else is wearing real Dittos or Levi’s with the red tab, and I’m stuck in these stiff off-brand ones with the weird patch pockets. I tried to fold the waistband down so they’d sit lower on my hips, but then my top rides up and you can see my stomach, which is completely gross and fat. I hate my body. I hate my hips, I hate my hair, I hate my nose. I look at the girls in *Seventeen* magazine and I don't understand how they look like women while I just look like a giant, clumsy mess.

When I walked through the front door, the house smelled like Mom’s Benson & Hedges and floor wax. She was sitting at the kitchen table under that ugly amber hanging lamp, doing her fingernails and listening to the radio. I stood in the doorway with my heavy binder, holding my breath, just hoping she’d look up and ask me how my day was. Just... really look at me. 

"Mom?" I said. 

She didn't even turn her head. She just blew on her nail polish and said, "Not now, sweetie, I've got a headache and your father's going to be late again." 

That was it. That's all I get. She didn't notice that I'd been crying in the girl's bathroom after third period, or that I wore my new top, or that I was practically vibrating with how miserable I feel every single second of the day. She’s always too tired, or too busy, or too wrapped up in her own life. It’s like she forgot what it feels like to be fourteen. Or maybe she just doesn't care. Maybe I’m just disappointing to her.

I came up to my room and locked the door. I put my headphones on—the big, heavy padded ones—and turned up my record player as loud as it goes so I don't have to listen to the silence in this house. I'm staring at the wood paneling on my wall, tracing the grain with my finger, wondering if anyone would even notice if I just stopped trying. If I just stopped talking completely. 

What is wrong with me? Why is it so easy for everyone to just look right through me?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
